nodes.title: Utah statute of limitations on a written-contract/credit-agreement consumer-debt lawsuit

derived_from.quoted_text: An action may be brought within six years: ... (b) subject to Subsection (2), upon any contract, obligation, or liability founded upon an instrument in writing, except those mentioned in Section 78B-2-311; or ...

For a credit agreement, as defined in Section 25-5-4, the six-year period described in Subsection (1) begins the later of the day on which: (a) the debt arose; (b) the debtor makes a written acknowledgment of the debt or a promise to pay the debt; or (c) the debtor or a third party makes a payment on the debt.

logic.applies_to: contracts/obligations founded on a written instrument -- most credit-card cardmember agreements and signed loan/retail-installment contracts qualify as 'credit agreements'
logic.accrual_for_credit_agreements: the LATEST of: (a) the day the debt arose, (b) the debtor's written acknowledgment of the debt or written promise to pay, or (c) the debtor's or a third party's payment on the debt -- meaning a payment or written acknowledgment can restart the accrual clock for a credit agreement specifically
logic.restart_risk_note: this restart mechanic is important and easy to miss: a debtor (or someone paying on their behalf) making even a partial payment, or signing anything acknowledging the debt, can reset the 6-year clock under subsection (2) -- debtors and their counsel should be cautious about payment or acknowledgment near the limitations boundary.
logic.determination: expired_if today > (latest_of[debt_arose_date, last_written_acknowledgment_date, last_payment_date] + 6 years), subject to any tolling not yet encoded

completeness_checklist.fact: Any written acknowledgment or written promise to pay by the debtor, and its date
Any payment made by the debtor or a third party on the debt, and its date

Whether the obligation is a 'credit agreement' under Section 25-5-4 (this node's accrual rule) vs. some other written contract (accrual would be the general contract-breach date instead, not separately encoded here)

consequences_and_next_steps.action: If 6 years have run from the latest of the three accrual triggers and no tolling applies, raise statute of limitations as an affirmative defense in the Answer.
Before assuming the SOL has run, confirm there is no later written acknowledgment or payment (including a third-party payment) that would restart the 6-year period under subsection (2).

nodes.title: Utah statute of limitations on an oral-contract or open-account consumer-debt lawsuit

derived_from.quoted_text: An action may be brought within four years: (1) after the last charge is made or the last payment is received: (a) upon a contract, obligation, or liability not founded upon an instrument in writing; (b) on an open store account for any goods, wares, or merchandise; or (c) on an open account for work, labor or services rendered, or materials furnished; ...

logic.applies_to: obligations not founded on a written instrument, plus open store accounts and open accounts for work/labor/services/materials
logic.accrual: explicitly the date of the LAST charge made or LAST payment received -- not the original debt date
logic.determination: expired_if today > (last_charge_or_payment_date + 4 years), subject to any tolling not yet encoded

completeness_checklist.fact: Date of the last charge made or last payment received on the account
Confirmation the obligation is genuinely not founded on a written instrument, or is an open store/services account (vs. UT-SOL-WRITTEN-CONTRACT-DEBT)

consequences_and_next_steps.action: If 4 years have run from the last charge or payment and no tolling applies, raise statute of limitations as an affirmative defense in the Answer.

nodes.title: Utah cap on wage garnishment for a consumer-credit-agreement judgment

derived_from.quoted_text: The maximum part of the aggregate disposable earnings of an individual for any pay period that is subjected to garnishment to enforce payment of a judgment arising from a consumer credit agreement may not exceed the lesser of: (a) 25% of the individual's disposable earnings for that pay period; (b) the amount by which the individual's disposable earnings for that pay period exceed 30 hours per week multiplied by the federal minimum hourly wage prescribed by Section 6(a)(1) of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, 29 U.S.C. Sec. 206(a)(1), in effect at the time the earnings are payable; or (c) 15% of the individual's disposable earnings for that pay period if the judgment relates to an education loan.
A court may not make, execute, or enforce an order or process in violation of this section.

logic.formula_ordinary_debt: min(25% of disposable earnings for the pay period, (disposable earnings - (30 x federal minimum hourly wage)))
logic.formula_education_loan: 15% of disposable earnings for the pay period, if the judgment relates to an education loan
logic.note: this is essentially Utah's conforming adoption of the federal CCPA formula (25% / 30x-minimum-wage) for ordinary consumer-credit judgments -- NOT more debtor-protective than the federal floor, unlike CA's post-SB-1477 formula (20%/48x) or TX's full wage-garnishment bar. A useful comparative note across the anchor states.
logic.note_needs_current_figure: this node encodes the FORMULA verbatim; the current federal minimum hourly wage figure needed to compute a dollar result must be pulled current at time of use, not hardcoded here.
logic.determination: max_garnishment_per_pay_period = the applicable lesser-of formula above; a court order exceeding it is unenforceable per subsection (3)

completeness_checklist.fact: Debtor's disposable earnings for the relevant pay period
Whether the underlying judgment is an ordinary consumer-credit-agreement debt (25%/30x formula) vs. an education loan (15% flat)
Current federal minimum hourly wage in effect when the earnings are payable

consequences_and_next_steps.action: If a garnishment order exceeds the applicable lesser-of formula, object citing Utah Code § 70C-7-103 -- subsection (3) makes an excess order unenforceable, not just voidable.

nodes.title: Utah homestead exemption from creditor execution

derived_from.quoted_text: (a) An individual is entitled to a homestead exemption consisting of property in this state in an amount not exceeding: (i) $5,000 in value if the property consists in whole or in part of property that is not the primary personal residence of the individual; or (ii) $42,000 in value if the property claimed is the primary personal residence of the individual. (b) If the property claimed as exempt is jointly owned, each joint owner is entitled to a homestead exemption, except that: (i) for property exempt under Subsection (2)(a)(i), the maximum exemption may not exceed $10,000 per household; or (ii) for property exempt under Subsection (2)(a)(ii), the maximum exemption may not exceed $84,000 per household.

A homestead is exempt from judicial lien and from levy, execution, or forced sale except for: (a) statutory liens for property taxes and assessments on the property; (b) security interests in the property and judicial liens for debts created for the purchase price of the property; (c) judicial liens obtained on debts created by failure to provide support or maintenance for dependent children; and (d) consensual liens obtained on debts created by mutual contract.

logic.inflation_adjustment: these dollar figures are the May 14, 2019 base amounts and are adjusted annually starting calendar year 2020 by a CPI-based formula in subsection (2)(e), published by the Utah State Auditor by January 1 of each year -- this node does NOT contain the current inflation-adjusted figure, only the base and the formula reference.
carveouts_not_protected: purchase-money security interests/judicial liens for the property's own purchase price
logic.determination: up to the applicable (and current, inflation-adjusted) exemption amount in home equity is protected from an ordinary judgment creditor's levy/execution/forced sale, subject to the four carveouts above

completeness_checklist.fact: Whether the property is the debtor's primary personal residence (higher exemption) or not (lower exemption)
Whether the property is jointly owned (affects the household cap)
Current CPI-adjusted dollar figures for the current calendar year (not the 2019 base amounts)
Whether the underlying debt/lien falls into one of the four carveout categories (not protected even if otherwise a homestead)

consequences_and_next_steps.action: If a creditor is attempting to force the sale of the debtor's home for an ordinary debt judgment (not one of the four carveout categories), claim the homestead exemption citing Utah Code § 78B-5-503.

nodes.title: Utah exemptions for household goods, tools of the trade, and a motor vehicle

derived_from.quoted_text: (1) An individual is entitled to exemption of the following property up to an aggregate value of items in each subsection of $1,000: (a) sofas, chairs, and related furnishings reasonably necessary for one household; (b) dining and kitchen tables and chairs reasonably necessary for one household; (c) animals, books, and musical instruments, if reasonably held for the personal use of the individual or the individual's dependents; and (d) heirlooms or other items of particular sentimental value to the individual. (2) An individual is entitled to an exemption, not exceeding $5,000 in aggregate value, of implements, professional books, or tools of the individual's trade, including motor vehicles to which no other exemption has been applied, and that are actually used by the individual in the individual's principal business, trade, or profession.
An individual is entitled to an exemption, not exceeding $3,000 in value, of one motor vehicle.

logic.tools_of_trade_note: can include a motor vehicle used in the debtor's principal business/trade/profession, but only 'to which no other exemption has been applied' -- i.e., cannot double-dip with the separate general vehicle exemption below
logic.general_motor_vehicle_note: excludes primarily-recreational vehicles (off-highway vehicles, most RVs), with carveouts for a motorcycle or van the debtor regularly uses for daily transportation
logic.determination: each category above is exempt up to its stated cap; a debtor cannot claim both the tools-of-trade vehicle exemption AND the general vehicle exemption for the same vehicle

completeness_checklist.fact: Value and category of household items at issue (which $1,000 sub-cap applies)
Whether a vehicle is claimed as a tool of the trade ($5,000 aggregate cap, business-use vehicles) vs. the general vehicle exemption ($3,000 cap) -- cannot claim both for the same vehicle
Whether a vehicle is primarily recreational (excluded from the general vehicle exemption, subject to the motorcycle/van daily-use carveout)

consequences_and_next_steps.action: If a creditor levies on household goods, trade tools, or a vehicle, claim the applicable exemption(s) citing Utah Code § 78B-5-506, being careful not to double-claim a single vehicle under both the tools-of-trade and general vehicle exemptions.

nodes.title: Utah deadline to respond to a debt-collection lawsuit summons and complaint

derived_from.quoted_text: Unless otherwise provided by statute or order of the court, a defendant must file and serve an answer within 21 days after the service of the summons and complaint within the state and within 30 days after service of the summons and complaint outside the state.

logic.trigger: date the summons and complaint are served on the defendant
logic.applies_to: general Utah district-court civil actions; small claims court uses a different, not-yet-built procedure
logic.determination: answer_due_date = date_of_service + (21 days if served within Utah, else 30 days if served outside Utah)

completeness_checklist.fact: Date the summons and complaint were actually served on the defendant
Whether service occurred within Utah (21 days) or outside Utah (30 days)
Whether the case is general district-court civil (this node) vs. small claims (different, not-yet-built procedure)

consequences_and_next_steps.action: File and serve a written Answer within 21 days of in-state service (30 days if served outside Utah) to avoid default.
consequences_and_next_steps.deadline_detail: 21 days from in-state service of summons and complaint, or 30 days if served outside Utah

consequences_and_next_steps.action: If already past the deadline and no default has been entered yet, respond immediately -- courts often still accept a late answer before default is entered.
